title: Investing in All of America Act of 2025
official_summary:
Investing in All of America Act of 2025

This bill modifies the limit on the amount of financing available to a Small Business Investment Company (SBIC) from the Small Business Administration (SBA). It also expands the definition of private capital with respect to SBICs.

Specifically, the bill reduces the maximum outstanding financing available to an SBIC from 300% to 200% of the SBIC's private capital. The bill increases from $350 million to $475 million the maximum financing available to two or more commonly controlled SBICs that make quarterly or semiannual interest payments.

The bill also expands the amounts that may be excluded from the calculation of the financing limit to include the amounts an SBIC invests in (1) rural areas, (2) certain technology categories, or (3) small manufacturers. The bill revises the cap on such excluded amounts to the lesser of $125 million or the aggregate of 50% of the private capital of the SBIC.

Additionally, the bill expands what is considered the private capital of an SBIC to include funds obtained from the business revenue of additional government-sponsored corporations and funds invested by the trust or endowment of a college or university.

summary.headline: New law changes how much federal-backed financing Small Business Investment Companies can get and what counts as their private capital.
summary.what_it_does: The law lowers the most SBA financing a Small Business Investment Company (SBIC) can have outstanding from 300% to 200% of its private capital, and raises the limit for groups of commonly controlled SBICs that pay interest quarterly or twice a year from $350 million to $475 million. Money an SBIC invests in rural areas, certain technology fields, or small manufacturers can be left out when figuring its limit, up to the lesser of $125 million or 50% of its private capital. It also lets SBICs count money from more government-sponsored corporations and from college or university trusts and endowments as private capital.

who_it_affects.how: Their maximum SBA financing is now tied to a lower multiple of private capital, with new exclusions for certain investments and broader sources counted as private capital.

who_it_affects.group: Small businesses in rural areas, certain technology fields, and small manufacturers
who_it_affects.how: SBIC investments in these businesses do not count toward the SBIC's financing limit, up to a cap.

who_it_affects.group: College and university trusts and endowments
who_it_affects.how: Money they invest in an SBIC can now count as that SBIC's private capital.
Funds from the business revenue of more of these corporations can now count as SBIC private capital.
The agency must apply the new financing limits and private capital rules when financing SBICs.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Enacted May 19, 2026; the summary does not give a separate effective date.
